d2-on-disk.title: On-disk layout and year file format

chapters.title: Overview: what it does for the business

phrases.text: This is a five-minute view of MarketStore, Alpaca's open-source database for financial time series. The voice explains, the code and the schemas follow, and after Play nothing needs to be pressed.
MarketStore is Alpaca's open-source database server for financial time series: price bars and ticks over many years, for all US equities and for crypto.

code.anchor: database server optimized for financial time-series data

phrases.text: This schema shows MarketStore in its environment: who talks to it, and where the data lives.
The client group contains the Python client, pymarketstore, a command-line shell, gRPC clients, and WebSocket subscribers. gRPC is a remote procedure call framework.

The server listens on JSON-RPC at port 5993 and on gRPC at port 5995, and it offers a stream endpoint for WebSockets and Prometheus metrics. JSON-RPC is another remote procedure call protocol, served here over HTTP.
Inside, one engine handles both queries and writes. Everything is stored under one data directory: a file per symbol, timeframe, attribute group and year, plus the write-ahead log.
Vendor data arrives through background-worker plugins. Configured triggers react asynchronously to normal writes; crash-WAL replay does not rerun them.
Replicas receive live WAL transaction groups over gRPC, normally port 5996. Their client-write restrictions have gaps in this release.

chapters.title: Main design ideas, requirements and assumptions

phrases.text: On disk, everything sits under the root directory, as a tree of folders: symbol, then timeframe, then attribute group.
At the bottom of the tree there is one file per year, for example 2017 dot bin. The write-ahead log file lives at the top.
Each year file starts with a fixed header of 37,024 bytes that describes its columns.
Fixed records occupy indexed slots. Variable records instead use 24-byte indirect slots pointing to payload data.
Intervals that were never written are holes in the file. Their index is zero, and the reader skips them.
Time selects the initial slot directly. Range reads still scan buffered slots and skip holes; variable data needs a second-stage read.

items.title: Idea 1: one file per series and year, positions computed from time

phrases.text: The 2016 design defines resolution as intervals per day. Intraday slot positions derive from time, rather than a search index.

code.anchor: Resolution is defined as number of time intervals stored per day

phrases.text: Intraday indexes count timeframes since January first, plus one. The daily branch instead uses day-of-year minus one; January first maps to zero, an important boundary concern.
IndexToOffset subtracts one before multiplying by record length and adding the header size. For a daily January first, index zero, that offset lands in the last bytes of the header.
The reader skips every slot whose index is zero, so January first in a daily file is never returned. This is read from the code, not observed in a run.

chapters.title: Workflows: call hierarchy, debug points, logs

phrases.text: The write path starts with a client sending a write request to the JSON-RPC endpoint.
The data service hands the columns to the writer's WriteCSM.
The writer finds the series in the catalog, or creates its directories and file, then checks and converts the data.
Writer.WriteRecords computes indexes and offsets, then queues the grouped commands in the WAL channel.

diagramFocus: RequestFlush(): wait unless flush already queued
phrases.text: RequestFlush usually waits for a requested flush. An already queued request returns immediately; without a background writer it flushes synchronously. Flush errors are logged, not propagated.

diagramFocus: MID TGDATA + TG length + TG + MD5
phrases.text: The group goes into the WAL file: a prepare marker, the data with an MD5 checksum, and a commit marker, followed by an fsync.

diagramFocus: (overwrite slot; page cache, no fsync here)
phrases.text: After WAL fsync, replication is enqueued and primary writes begin. Fixed records overwrite slots; variable records merge payloads through an indirect slot.
Normal flush dispatches triggers asynchronously. Client success does not unconditionally prove durability or completed derived updates.
Scenario two is a write. The client sends a msgpack write request to slash rpc. DataService Write converts each dataset and calls WriteCSM.

phrases.text: WriteCSM looks the series up in the catalog, or, on a first write, creates its directories and its year file.
FlushToWAL drains the queue into one transaction group and writes the prepare marker.

diagramFocus: MID TGDATA + TG length + TG + MD5
phrases.text: Normal flush writes the group, checksum and commit marker, then fsyncs the WAL. Replication and primary writes follow; trigger records are dispatched even after a logged primary-write failure.
Variable writes read existing payload, optionally decompress it, and append incoming events before sorting.
They sort by timestamp, optionally Snappy-compress, write the merged tail payload, and update the indirect index/offset/length slot.

That was the view mode. The full walk has six chapters and about thirty-seven minutes. In it you can pause, ask a question at any place, or press D to stop and discuss, and the walk is amended and continues where you were.
